utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, could you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you and good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-03-67-T, the Prosecutor versus Vojislav Seselj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Registrar. This is Tuesday, October 14th, 2008, and I welcome the representatives of the OTP as well as those helping us. I welcome Mr. Seselj and everyone helping us in this courtroom. Today, we will have a witness scheduled to come in the courtroom soon. Let me remind you that the Prosecution has set aside two hours for examination-in-chief, unless I'm mistaken. Defence will therefore be granted two hours for the cross-examination. On the last day of the week, we will have a 92 ter witness, so we'll have a witness under Rule 92 ter. Mr. Seselj, I believe that you have a few things to say, so you have the floor quickly.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Two things, very briefly. First of all, the OTP, through the prison guards, tried on Friday and on Monday to deliver the very same documents to me on CD-ROM, which I categorically refused. I noticed in passing that the documents have to do with the expert report of Ewa Tabeau, but I don't know what the contents are. They did that in spite of your ruling that all documents be submitted to me on paper. Secondly, you probably remember that a few times I demanded that Witness VS-1031 testifies viva voce rather than as a 92 ter witness. Yesterday, I received from the OTP yet another request to have this witness testify as a 92 ter witness. The date is the 25th of September; of the request, that is, and it was delivered to me only yesterday. This time, I can just respond straight away orally to this request in order to speed up the proceedings, because the witness is supposed to come in about 15 days or so, that the witness can testify as a 92 ter witness in view of the command position he had at the time. It would truly be ludicrous if this witness were to come as a 92 ter witness. So if you look at what his statement has to do with, all of it will be clear to you. Not to dwell on it any longer. I think that you had a look at it yourselves and have seen for yourselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We will look into this. Very quickly now, for Ewa Tabeau, this question of the CD-ROMs, can you tell us what this is all about, Ms. Dahl?

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry. I'm not able to answer your question at the moment. I'll need to find out what was disclosed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let's bring the witness into the courtroom, then, and we will ask him to take the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, sir. Could you please give us your name, surname, and date of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am Franja Baricevic, born on the 3rd of June, 1953, in Hrtkovci.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is your job at the moment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm a mechanic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Have you ever testified in front of a national or international court regarding what happened in former Yugoslavia, or is this the first time that you are testifying in court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is my first time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You may read the declaration that is in front of you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just need to get my glasses. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You may sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me give you a few details regarding the way this hearing is going to happen. This is the first time you're testifying in court, and it is usually something that is quite striking for anyone. My mission first is to reassure you and to tell you exactly what is going to happen. You will be asked questions by the representative of the OTP, and you have to answer these questions. I'm sure that you have met this person either this morning or yesterday in order to prepare for this hearing. The Prosecutor may also present a few documents to you. After this phase, Mr. Seselj, who is on your left, and I'm sure you know who it is, will be putting questions to you, and this will be the cross-examination. He will be entitled to put questions to you. Most of these questions are aimed at testing your credibility and also at addressing issues of substance that were dealt with during the examination-in-chief. The three Judges on the Bench in front of you can also take the floor at any moment if they need some details on subjects that are not clear enough. Please try to be very specific in your answers. If at one point in time you do not understand the question, just ask the person putting the question to you to rephrase it. Even if it's a Judge, don't hesitate to ask the Judge to reformulate the question. You cannot answer a question correctly if you have not understood it perfectly. We will have 20-minute breaks every hour and a half, so which means that we'll soon have a break in about an hour or so. You have made a solemn declaration, so you're now the witness of justice. You will no longer be in contact with the OTP. If we're able to finish this hearing today, so much the better. If not, we will continue tomorrow, which means that you will have to come in this courtroom again tomorrow afternoon, but you're not supposed to have any contact with the OTP in the meanwhile. The Trial Chamber, of course, can answer any questions you may wish, if need be. I wanted to say all this to make sure that this hearing would run as smoothly as possible. Good afternoon, Mr. Prosecutor, and you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everybody in the courtroom. I have two issues to raise before I start the examination-in-chief. Please allow me to introduce Mr. Christian Simon. He's sitting here with us. He is and intern and helped in the preparation. And another issue is I think I will not need two hours, but I can do this examination-in-chief in about 90 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. Baricevic, good afternoon. First of all, I would like to tell the Judges your private and professional background. So could you please tell us, what is your nationality, and what is your ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: I'm a Croat, Catholic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Are you married, and do you have children?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: I'm married. My wife's name is Jadranka. I have a daughter and a son. The daughter was born in 1978 and the son in 1983. I live in Jaksic. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Could you please let us know in which country is this village is situated?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: The village is in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Did you always live in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: No, no. Until the 19th of May, 1992, I lived in Hrtkovci, in Vojvodina. The address was Savska, number 19.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Can you please let us know, since when did you live in Hrtkovci?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: I lived in Hrtkovci from my birth, 1953, up until the date that I've already told you about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Have your parents already lived in Hrtkovci?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: My mother -- or, rather, my great-grandfather, grandfather and mother always lived in Hrtkovci, whereas my father originally came from Lika, present-day Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Could you please let us know what was your occupation or your work in Hrtkovci?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: Well, actually, I completed secondary school in Hrtkovci. Actually, it was a 3-year vocational school in Ruma. Then I went to do my military service in Sombor. I did my training over two and a half months' time, and after that I was transferred to Tuzla. So that went on for 15 months. Afterwards, I went to Zagreb. I worked for the railways there. I completed some vocational training there at the railways, that is to say, to drive motor vehicles. I spent three years there. After three years, I went back to Hrtkovci where I started working for the waterworks. I worked there as a maintenance worker up until 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Have you ever been engaged in politics?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: While I was still doing my military service, I was a member of the Communist Party, all the way up to the death of Josip Broz Tito. When he died, I returned my membership card and I never joined any party afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: So you were never afterwards in a political party, but did you engage in political affairs on the local level?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Sorry. I don't know if you --

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know how you're going to understand this. I was just a member of the Assembly of the Local Commune. A member of the Assembly of the Local Commune, well, that is an organ that governs the local commune, that takes care of the functioning of the local commune, basic care concerning the local commune. It's not really a political party, no. That's what I did, and the term of office was four years.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One small detail. You told us that you were a member of the Communist Party. At the time, out of 100 people, how many were members of the Communist Party; 10 per cent, 20 per cent, 50 per cent? Was it only a minority that was in the Communist Party or other?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you know what? Most people who, well, worked for the municipality and the local commune were supposed to be members of the party in order to get a job. This was an unwritten rule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I understood you right, you were a member of the Communist Party for your job, not for ideological reasons.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right. That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. Baricevic, do you know how many inhabitants Hrtkovci had at the time?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't quite understand you. What time do you mean? You mean when I got my job with the local commune or when? Later in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: No, in 1990.

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: In the 1990s, our village had a population of 2.900, roughly, perhaps -- well, give or take an inhabitant or two.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Do you know what the ethnic distribution was in your village? I guess there was more than one.

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: There were 13 different ethnicities in our village. 75 per cent were Croats and Hungarians, and 25 per cent were all the rest -- well, all the rest.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Do you know how many -- what was the percentage of the Serb ethnicity among this 25 per cent?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: Well, the Serb ethnicity were, well, about 25 per cent, so 5 per cent would be all the rest -- I mean, well, Romanians and all the rest.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Can you describe the relationship between the different ethnicities before 1990?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. You know what? Well, this village was a village of industrious people, a calm and peaceful place. When you'd arrive there, you wouldn't know who was who. All of these people were hardworking. They worked day in, day out, and no distinctions were made in terms of ethnicity or anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Had there been any tensions between the ethnicities?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: Well, ethnic tensions started -- well, it is a well-known fact that Milosevic held his rallies all the way from Kosovo to Vojvodina. Then in the village, well, he pulled some people -- I don't know how to put this. There is chafe in every wheat, if I can put it that way. But, you know, people didn't really pay much attention to these people who were becoming louder and louder.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Did I understand you correct that before Milosevic had these rallies, the relationship between the ethnicities was okay; there were no tensions?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: That's right. That's right. It was peaceful. As I've already said, everything was fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: And can you tell us when there was a change? Can you give us the year, probably?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: Well, as I said, when Milosevic organised these rallies, then this party was established, Vuk Draskovic's party and Seselj's party, you know, and then people -- well, how should I put this? People who were in favour of that party were already apart from the rest, and they started creating some trouble and whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Do you know when Seselj's party was erected in Hrtkovci?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: Well, sometime in 1991, a branch was established in the village, of Seselj's party, that is. First of all, Aco Ejic founded this party or these parties, and Ostoja Sibincic founded the SPO; and then Aco Ejic gave up, and Sibincic espoused the SPO. I mean, he was in Seselj's party. I am sorry, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: We'll come to this later. Can you give us the reasons why these tensions arose?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't quite understand you. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: You told us -- I'll summarise it. You told us until 1990, the relationship was okay between the different ethnicities; and from 1991 onwards, there was a rise of tension or there were first tensions, and I want to know from you what was the reason for these tensions.

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: Just a minute, please. The tensions started when this party was established. At first, these refugees came in. This group of 160 refugees came from Slavonia, and then, well, then the tensions started among the people there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Can you please tell us, what were these refugees and where did they come from? You already said "Slavonia," but what was the reason that they came, and what kind of people were these?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: Well, you know what? This first wave of refugees -- just a moment, please. This first wave of refugees arrived from Slavonia. Just a moment. Sorry. This first wave of refugees arrived from Slavonia, and then the local Commune of Hrtkovci found some kind of shelter for these people, and, also, food aid was given to them. We collected food for them. The local commune even bought stoves for them, for those people who didn't have stoves in their homes, and in that way they were taken care of. Even financial contributions were given for these people who said that they didn't have any money.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Was there enough room for all the refugees in Hrtkovci in the beginning?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: No. Well, a few remained, but, you know, they had some relatives -- well, there wasn't enough room for them, you know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, is this still 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's already the beginning of 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A small mystery that I haven't been able to solve until now. These refugees came from Slavonia, but why did they arrive in your village? Couldn't they go elsewhere? Is it because your village was on the way from Slavonia? Why is it that they ended up in your village? Why didn't they directly go to Belgrade? Why did they stop in your village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, this is something I find unclear, too, but I will tell you that they were channeled, in a way. They reported to this president, this president of that branch, I mean, and he channeled them to different places. I cannot tell you what the connection was, but at any rate, all of them came to Hrtkovci. Now, I cannot say that this or that person asked them to come. I cannot tell you about the first group, what the reason was, but I did know that they all turned to Ostoja Sibincic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: You already mentioned Ostoja Sibincic. Could you please describe us the role he had at that time in the village?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: Ostoja Sibincic, well, I know him very well. He's just a bit older than I am. He completed some military academy, and then he was thrown out of there, and then he came to Ruma to work as a municipality clerk, and he led Seselj's party there. He was a very active member.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Was he in Seselj's -- Mr. Seselj's party from the beginning, or was he in another party? Do you remember this?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I've already said. First, he espoused the SPO; and then briefly, he went to Seselj's party.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Do you know him personally?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: Oh, yes, personally. I live in one street, and he lives in this other street. I've known him very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Can you please tell us a bit about his political attitude, if you know this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, if I may. This switch from one party to another, when did it occur?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wouldn't know the date, you know, but it was towards the end of 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecution and the Judges are asking very important questions for us. I mean, they are crucial for us. We need to know when the Serbian Radical Party actually had a seat and had recognition. I'm listening to you. You're saying that Mr. Seselj had a party and this and that. This is not enough for us. We need to have dates. We need to know the exact date at which this happened, and we need to know exactly why you know that this is Mr. Seselj's party. So could you please enlighten us on this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I don't know the exact dates, but it was towards the end of 1991. And he always stressed that he was a radical, and the -- he didn't have the headquarters of his party there, but the meetings were held in his apartment. His apartment was smack in the middle of the village, you know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. Baricevic, you described Mr. Sibincic as a radical. Do you remember if he gave a specific name to Serbs who had a friendly relationship to Croats at that time?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: Well, as I've already said, I was a member of the Local Commune Assembly, and there was this meeting that we held that was attended by Ostoja Sibincic. The president of the Local Commune Assembly was a Serb, an ethnic Serb, Dobrosav Markovic, and he told him this: He said, "What kind of Serbs are you when you've been able to live side by side with Ustashas for such a long time?"

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Do you know the expression he used? If you don't remember, it doesn't matter, but do you remember?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. He said that the local indigenous Serbs were low-quality Serbs, whereas the Serbs that had come from Slavonia, he said that they were good-quality Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Why were the local Serbs qualified as low-quality Serbs?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: Well, that was because they got along well with Croats. As I've already explained, they lived in a brotherly fashion. They helped each other. This was a village of industrious people, people who got along well with each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: You already mentioned it. How was Ostoja Sibincic involved in the housing problems? Can you please describe it a bit broader?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: Well, as I've already explained, all those people, all those refugees turned to him personally, and he provided them with addresses of people who were working abroad in Germany, Italy, France, Belgium, the Netherlands, all over Europe; and they left those houses there to their family, to their neighbours, for safekeeping, so to speak. But they would come back to spend their annual leave there in those houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: And what did Ostoja Sibincic propose to locate the refugees?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: Well, his proposal was that those people should move in, but the local commune could not dispose of other people's property without the approval of the owner.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: So this was also a reason that tensions arose?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that was a reason for the tensions. People had to start locking their doors and report to other people what the situation was like in the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Do you remember names of persons who came -- of refugees who came from Slavonia to Hrtkovci? Do you remember specific names?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I do know that there was this man, Rade Cakmak. Yes, I'm able to recall this one name. He broke into a house owned by a man who worked in Germany at the time. The house was locked up. It was full of all kinds of things because this man had worked in Germany for 30 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Did there come a moment when this housing situation in Hrtkovci became critical with the arrival of refugees from Slavonia?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: Well, the situation became critical because of the unrest that was generated in the village. People were simply upset; they felt uneasy. And the people who had come from Slavonia, they were also looking for some kind of a solution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Do you know if promises have been made to these refugees related to their accommodation?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: Those refugees had been duped. They had been told that the houses would be empty, that the people from Hrtkovci had gone to join the Ustashas. But when they came, there were people living in those houses, working, living in the houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Did the refugees complain about the situation?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. They demanded a meeting with Seselj. They wanted Seselj to attend the meeting. But on Easter -- rather, on Good Friday, an activist, a female activist from Ruma came. I don't know her name, but she came to attend this meeting that was held in the culture hall in Hrtkovci.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. Baricevic, what I'd like to know is: From where do you know that refugees complained about the situation? Can you let us know?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: Well, of course I know. When I worked in the local commune, I was there all the time with all of them, and I knew that a meeting would be held because I had the keys to the hall. In fact, I kept the keys for all the important buildings in Hrtkovci because I was in the local commune, so they came to me to ask me for the keys in order to be able to hold the meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, Witness. What my colleague was saying, well, the same thing crossed my mind. What we need to know are the dates. This meeting was held in the presence of this woman coming from Ruma. On what date?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was the Catholic Easter, the Good Friday. The Good Friday, to be more specific.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1998, in April, since it was Easter for the Catholics. We'll check.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was the Good Friday. That's the most specific --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Another point also. You said that they had been tricked. When I heard you say that, I wondered who they had been duped by; the Croats who had told them to leave and, "You will find houses in Hrtkovci," or by Serbs, who told them that they would find houses in Hrtkovci? Who tricked them, exactly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I've already said Serbs, of course, because they had told them that Croats had gone to Croatia to join the Ustashas, the army. You know, that's what they said. They said that the houses were empty. The local -- the local authorities, they most likely duped them because they told the refugees that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In other words, by Serbs from Slavonia, those were the people that purportedly --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Let's come back to Good Friday in April 1991. You described that a female activist arrived in Hrtkovci --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, it wasn't in 1991. It was in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. It was a mistake. I mean 1992. Thank you for correcting me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: You told us that the refugees were not satisfied with what this female activist told them. Did they have another wish, who should come to Hrtkovci to resolve or to care about their problems?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: After that -- they were unhappy, and after that they demanded to meet with Seselj. They wanted Seselj to come personally to the village and to hold this meeting with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Why did they ask that Mr. Seselj should come to Hrtkovci?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what happened at that meeting, but people were really dissatisfied, unhappy. They wanted this meeting to be held, and it was finally held on the 6th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Okay, we come to this later. But could you please let us know, was there a kind of preparation for this rally before Mr. Seselj arrived?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Throughout the day, there was Chetnik music blaring from the loudspeakers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, Witness. Since we are dealing with extremely important issues, it is important to take this step by step and not make a mistake. I listened very carefully to what you're saying, therefore. If I have understood correctly, dissatisfied Serbs wanted to meet Mr. Seselj, and then a woman comes from Ruma --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- and those people who wanted to meet Seselj don't meet him, since it is a woman who comes. And you say that the meeting of the 6th of May was then organised. We know that on the 6th of May, Mr. Seselj delivered a speech. So how do you know that all this happened, i.e., that the dissatisfied Serbs want to see Mr. Seselj, and instead, the woman from Ruma comes, and the meeting of the 6th of May is organised? How do you know that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I've already said. I worked in the village. I talked to people. I worked with them, and it's a village. People talk about stuff, and the word gets 'round. And I've already told you that I had given them the keys to the culture hall where the meeting was held with this woman, and I started to recount how, as far as the 6th of May is concerned, I gave them the PA system from the culture hall, and this was something that was bought by the Local Commune Assembly to be put at the disposal of all the political parties. All of them were given the right to some space and to the PA system.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, we know, since we've heard other witnesses, the Bench already have some evidence. We know that there was an election campaign at the time. Therefore, as part of the election campaign, politicians like Mr. Seselj come to one or other village to hold speeches in view of the upcoming elections. You are stating that the meeting of the 6th of May has nothing to do with the election campaign, if I understand you correctly, but had to do with those dissatisfied Serbs who wanted to meet Mr. Seselj. According to you, there are two reasons. Either it is due to the political campaign, and that is why Mr. Seselj was there, or it was because those dissatisfied Serbs wanted to meet Mr. Seselj. So what is the reason, according to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely. They wanted to meet Mr. Seselj so that he could give them some guidelines how to proceed, to put it quite simply.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, but since Mr. Seselj did not hold an official position in the local commune -- was that the case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, they demanded to meet with somebody higher up in the Radical Party. They were unhappy with Ostoja Sibincic. They wanted to talk to somebody higher up to give them some guidelines as to how to proceed, what they should do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: I was asking if there was a kind of preparation for this rally, and you started before the Presiding Judge asked you an additional question. But there was music. Was there also more? What was this preparation; can you tell us?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: Well, there was music and there were posters all over the streets, and across the road from the gas station there was some kind of a platform put up. A trailer was dragged there, and then the sides were put down, and this was some kind of a scene.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Where was it in the village; can you let us know?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: Well, it was in Vladimir Nazor Street. Let me think about the number. 15, near the number 15. There was the intersection. Well, that's where most -- where there was a lot of space, and the lawn that was across the road from the gas station was used to put up this stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Before Mr. Seselj arrived the 6th of May, did there arrive, also, other people to the village?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: A bus came in.(redacted)

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: (redacted), and there were White Eagles on the bus. They said that they were there as Seselj's security detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: From where do you know that these were White Eagles?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: Well, they wore black uniforms, and they had rifles.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: But there were also other people who had black uniforms and rifles. This does not explain to me why these should have been White Eagles.

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: Well, they said they were the White Eagles, that they were Seselj's security.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Do you know of a political group which is asserted -- which the White Eagles are asserted to, the White Eagles belong to?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: Well, what is the name of it? Let me think just a moment. What was it that they said?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: If you don't remember, we'll come to the next question. It's not that important for me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I'd like to get back to something which is extremely important, which you mentioned at the first time we hear this and deserves our attention. You said that these men dressed in black and that had rifles were the White Eagles. You said they were in charge of Mr. Seselj's security. When you say "they," is it something they said -- told you directly, or was this something you heard from someone else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, they didn't tell me personally, but they said -- well, they were -- there were people there at the gas station, and they told them. They didn't tell me personally, but I was there close by, and they were guarding the area around the gas station and the stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I understand you correctly, there was a group of people standing next to the petrol station. Then the White Eagles arrive, and they tell this group standing there that they were in charge of Mr. Seselj's security. And you hear someone from the group saying this to you, or were they talking amongst themselves and that is something which you overheard? Is this how things happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, yes, they talked, and that's how I learnt about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Had you heard about the White Eagles before that time, or was it the first time you saw them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You mean in the village?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, in the village.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ... time. The first time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But before that time, were the White Eagles well known?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, people didn't know about them, but they had never been to the village. That was the first time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What did people say about these men; good things or bad things?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Bad things. Bad things were said about those people. They were not an army at all. They had long hair. They were disheveled. They were dressed in all kinds of clothes. Some people wore boots, some other kind of footwear. You could see that this was not a regular, proper army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry. There's something I don't understand. When the local municipality is informed that a political party is organising a rally and decides to provide what is necessary in support of this rally, is the local police also informed about this; in other words, that the police needs to stand guard in the village? Was the local police there, and if the local police were there, this meant that a group which did not belong to the local police could be in charge of law and order in Hrtkovci?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I understand your question. There was police, but the police did not attend the rally, the police that belonged to the authorities at the time. They were about a kilometre away from the area, and they were regulating traffic, so one kilometre away at both sides. So all they did was just regulate the traffic. They were not there at the rally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. That's clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Did you, yourself, go to the rally?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: I did attend this rally there where the gas station was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Why did you go there?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I was curious as to what would be done with Croats because I had heard all kinds of stories, and then I said to myself, well, let's go there, and let's see what will be decided. I was simply curious.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Did you go alone, or were you accompanied by someone?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: No, I did not go there alone. My brother, my half-brother, Ladislav Hunjadi from France had come on his vacation, so we had lunch together, and I said, "Well, brother, it seems that this is the last time that you've come to visit me." So he looked at me. He didn't get what I was saying. And then I told him, "Well, you'll see after this rally, sure enough."

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Why did you have this feeling? Can you explain this?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: Well, as I've already told you, if one lives in the village, works side by side with people, you can see how they're thinking, and you do realise what's going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Do you know how many people, approximately, participated at that rally?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: Well, there were quite a few people. People came in from all over the place, from various villages. There were about 2.000 people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Do you know who gave a speech during this rally? Can you tell us?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: Well, the rally was opened by Milan Zilic. The stage was actually set up in front of his house.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Can you please describe us the stage, how it was constructed, what kind of stage it was?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: Well, as I've already explained, it was a trailer that was dragged there by a tractor, and then the sides were put down, and some kind of a lectern was put there for the speakers to use.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Did Mr. Zilic mention names of the Hrtkovci inhabitants?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zilic made a speech, and he mentioned the names of people who had already been in Croatia; some of them in Croatia, some of them in Germany, some of them in Austria, that is. Well, if necessary, I'll give you the names: Sostaric, the Grdic brothers, the Cindric brothers, Stepic, Markus, Mate Markus, and the rest. He said that they had joined the ZNG and that they were attacking Serbs with Ustasha knives. That is how he described the situation and these people while he made his speech.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Did he say what should happen to these people or these families?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, everything you're saying is of utmost importance. To make sure that you don't make assumptions, let me tell you that we have the speeches made by the three speakers. We have their speeches, and I've just noted that you said something that was not in the speech. At one point in time, you said that Mr. Zilic talked about the Ustashi knives. Are you absolutely sure you heard it with your own ears?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're completely sure?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm quite sure. Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What exactly did he say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These were the first people whose names were called out at the beginning of the speech. It was stated that they were in the ZNG and that they were attacking people with Ustasha knives.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is it "knife," or is it -- what kind of knife is it, this Ustasha knife?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I never saw this type of knife before, so I don't know what he meant. That's what he said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, allow me to correct. We have Mr. Seselj's published speech which Mr. Seselj published in his books. It's the Prosecution -- just to be correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, can I ask you, now that you mention the version of the speech which we have seen in Mr. Seselj's book, do you know if there exists a recording -- an audio-recording of the speech, and if so, if that audio-recording has been typed out?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: What I can tell you is that the Prosecution tried for more than two years to get this audio record of the speech, which allegedly exists. We never could find it. When Mr. Seselj was testifying in Milosevic, he said three times that he has the video of the speech and that he will use this video during his case. At that moment, we gave up because we had -- we said that it's important that the truth comes out. We cannot find this speech. Very strange things happened when we tried to get it. There were archives burned down and so on, so we gave up, and we didn't -- we don't have the speech. We have what Mr. Seselj published. We are informed that this is in his book. I don't remember the title, but it was published when he was already in detention. We don't know a further version. We have got from Mr. Seselj the 80 books, which he gave to us in October of 2003. We were very carefully looking through these books. We couldn't find it. Maybe that we over-read it, but I would be very grateful to Mr. Seselj if he could show us where it is published in these books.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, last time you told us that you had the video. Of course, you said that you were not going to cooperate with the OTP and you had no intention of disclosing this to the OTP. But it's important, so the Trial Chamber now is turning to you. If you have the video and the audiotape that goes along with it, please give it. It could be very useful for you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have the video-recording, and I had intended to use it in the cross-examination of Witness Aleksa Ejic. However, as you know, all my communications with my associates, with my Defence team, with my legal advisers have been cut off, and I am not in a position to use that video clip. However, Mr. Mussemeyer would have to say whose archives, when, where; and Mr. Mussemeyer would have to review those 80 books that I handed in here in the courtroom in 2003 to counsel for the Prosecution. They contain the entire transcript of the rally from Hrtkovci. These are paperbacks. Mr. Mussemeyer has a new edition of my complete works, hardcover ones that were published after went to The Hague. However, the paperback ones were published before I came to The Hague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Mussemeyer, those archives which burned down, or I don't know what -- what exactly are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: What I'm talking about is that we tried to get in possession of the video and the speech, and we did not succeed. We were trying hard to find it over there in, let's say, Austria, in Germany and France. We were trying specifically in Serbia, but we never could find this video. And when we contacted a television station, it was -- in one case, it was said that the archive burned down. On other occasions, we were told that the tapes have been used for next little video clips because there were not enough tapes. The result is we never got in possession of this video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, let's not give up hope. Maybe Mr. Seselj's associates will soon send it, and we'll be able to look at it and see it. Let's not give up any hope.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: A little observation. We were looking very carefully through all these 80 books. It doesn't mean that I personally did it. As you know, I unfortunately don't speak B/C/S, but we have analysts who were reading through all the books. They had a specific view of Hrtkovci, and they couldn't find it. It's possible that they overread it, so it would be great if Mr. Seselj could tell us in which book it was published, that we can come with the real version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, in which book is it? In which book is this speech?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot remember exactly in which book out of the 80 concerned. However, the title is not "Speeches in Hrtkovci" but "The Major Importance of the May Elections," so they can search under that heading. That's how it was published.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So it is "The Major Importance of the Speeches of the May Election" or something like that. Very well. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. Baricevic, let's come back to the speech of Milan Zilic. You told us that he was mentioning family names of Hrtkovci inhabitants. Was your name also mentioned by him?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: No, no. My speech was -- my name was not mentioned in that speech made by Milan Zilic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Who spoke after Mr. Zilic has finished his speech?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: Some woman that I didn't know. I don't know what her name was, but she spoke very briefly. I mean, she did not make a very long speech. She made a very short speech.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Who spoke next?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: After her, Seselj spoke, Vojislav Seselj.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Could you see and hear him clearly?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I've already said that I was 30 or 40 metres away from the stage, and things could be heard quite clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Do you remember the main topics of Mr. Seselj's speech?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I remember. At any rate, in the beginning, well, something was wrong with the loudspeakers, and then he asked for the -- for the loudspeakers to be switched off and to remove the ropes that they had placed there. Afterwards, the speech started with the well-known borders, Virovitica, Karlobag and whatever else, whatever it was that he said, as he did say, as he presented these borders of this future Greater Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Has he also mentioned names in his speech?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: Well, as I said, he spoke. He made this short speech, and then after that, after that, the names of the top people in the village. Well, that's what he called out: Mato Samov [phoen], Franjo Samov [phoen], Dr. Branko Vuksanic, Zdenko Barisic, head of the local office. Among them, he called out my name, too, and others.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Do you remember when --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute. You heard the speech. You listened very carefully to the speech, right? You said that you came out of curiosity, that you were 30 metres away from Mr. Seselj, but you listened very carefully to the speech. And do you remember the speech well, as of now? Let me read a passage from this speech, and I would like to have your opinion on this. This is what he says: "We must maintain the existence of Yugoslavia because it will then be much easier for Serbs from Krajina and from the Serbian Bosnia-Herzegovina to integrate Yugoslavia as a federal entity, much easier than if we had proclaimed the state of Serbia and if they had had to integrate the state later on at a later stage. In this respect, to integrate Yugoslavia, all they will have to do is say that they never left it; and thanks to this, they will be in a much better position on the international scene." So here, he spoke about Yugoslavia in this speech, and it seems that he told everyone he was talking to that he was in favour of Yugoslavia being maintained as it was. Do you remember this; and if so, what did you think of that at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't remember that. I do remember that he said, "Serb Dubrovnik, Serb Karlovac, Serb Virovitica." Just a moment, please. Well, that's the kind of thing he said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You don't remember the other part. Very well. Mr. Prosecutor, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: You mentioned that you also heard your name from Mr. Seselj's mouth; is that correct, just to summarise if I understood it correctly?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Did he give the reason what should happen to these people he was reading out?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: Well, he said that Serb refugees did not have a roof over their heads and that Croats had to leave the village within three days. They would get keys and addresses, and they'd have to leave the village. If they didn't want to do that, they will load them onto a bus and send them to the border. "Let them go to their beautiful homeland." Well, their homeland, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Do we have an idea where Mr. Seselj got these names? He is not from Hrtkovci.

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: Well, of course he's not. Ostoja Sibincic, the top people gave him that list, the top people of that political party.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Is that your assumption, or do you know this for certain?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: I know that for sure because Seselj didn't even know who held what position, who had what job, and he read everything out very exactly and specifically.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, here, again, you are addressing a very important topic. In the speech that we have, which is an extract of Mr. Seselj's book, this is not mentioned. There could be two reasons for this: Either in the excerpts that he published in his book, he slightly tampered his speech and took out the passage you mentioned; or the second reason is that you could be adding things in his mouth, putting things in his mouth. I'm putting a question again to you, and it's very important. Are you absolutely sure that during this speech Mr. Seselj read out a list of names of people living in your village who were Croats and who had to leave? Are you 100 per cent sure that he read out this list?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm perfectly sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 100 per cent sure. So when he published the book, he tampered with the truth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, at any rate, he read out these people's names, and these people moved out of the village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, could you give us the difference between the list that was read out by Zilic and the list read out by Mr. Seselj?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll tell you very gladly. What Mr. Zilic read out were the names of people who were already in Germany and Austria and in Croatia, who had been working there for years, whereas these people whose names Seselj read out, these people worked in Hrtkovci, lived there. At that time, they were still working there, at the time when the rally was held.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's assume that you were telling the truth. Mr. Seselj delivered a speech and reads out names. As far as you recollect, what happened? Did he take out a piece of paper from his pocket to read out that list, or did he give all those names while he was speaking from the top of his head?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I didn't see him take it out of his pocket, this list, I mean. However, I do know that these people had their names called out and that he could not have known the names of people who had lived there. It's the top people from the village who wrote this up for him and gave it to him to read.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So if you're telling the truth, this means that before delivering his speech, Mr. Seselj spoke with the leaders, and the leaders gave him a list. Then he, who knows absolutely no one in this village - this is the first time that he set foot in this village - just out of -- from memory, he was able to give five or ten -- between five to ten names, which means that he learned five to ten names by rote so that he could actually speak them out in his speech, because in the speech that I have, he mentioned a great number of people, but people who had nothing to do with the village. For example, he mentioned members of the Communist League, Vuk Draskovic, Milan Komenic, Dragoljub Misilevic [phoen], Zoran Djindjic, Kosta Kovarski [phoen], Nikola Milosevic. So he mentioned a great number of names. So he's very good at quoting names of people that he knows for political reasons, of course, but he didn't know the names of the villagers in the first place. That means that if you're telling the truth, he learned by rote five to ten names and then delivered them in a speech. Is this what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to say something to you. Ostoja Sibincic was Seselj's right-hand man. Most probably, he had contacted him - every day, that is - in terms of what the situation in the village was like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So you think that Ostoja Sibincic was in permanent contact with Mr. Seselj, and that's how he learned those names. That may be what happened. I mean, as a Judge, I have to look into all possibilities. Mr. Mussemeyer, we have seven to eight minutes left before the break. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. Baricevic, did Mr. Seselj also speak about mixed marriages in his speech? Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: He did speak, yes, and he said the following: Mixed marriages should be divorced, and children from mixed marriages should be killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Are you sure about this?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: 100 per cent sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: I will come now to the time after the speech. Mr. Baricevic, can you tell us how the atmosphere --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute, Mr. Prosecutor. I'd like to come back to this because this is also essential. You heard distinctively that Mr. Seselj was saying that children from mixed marriage should be killed? I mean, this is terrible, and this is spoken in front of 2.000 people. You're saying "2.000," and another witness said there were only 700 people in attendance. So he did utter those words? It's not in the book, in the speech that's in the book. I can tell you that right away. You're absolutely sure that you heard that? One question in passing. Were there any reporters present? The day after the speech, was there any reports of the speech in the papers or excerpts of the speech in the papers? Did the radio talk about it, saying that Mr. Seselj came to Hrtkovci to make a speech and so forth and so on? Were there any reports on this speech? This is a politician on May 6th, 1992. If he said that children from mixed marriage should be killed, this should be in the front page of all papers in the world. So I would like to know whether any reporters were present at the time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't see the journalists, but afterwards I saw that the rally was written about. "Borba" wrote about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Borba"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The reporter must have been there, probably.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Later on, I read that they had written about that rally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the local police who was regulating traffic, could they hear the PA system? Could they hear the speech through the PA system at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that Seselj had said to turn off the loudspeakers and to remove the ropes. I don't think that the local police guarded this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Prosecutor, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: How much time do I have until the break? Five minutes or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Three minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: I will continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: I wanted to ask the witness if there was any change of atmosphere after Mr. Seselj was gone and has delivered the speech.

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: After this speech, the situation in the village became very heated. People -- or rather, groups of people broke into houses. They forced people out of their homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Did you and/or other inhabitants of Hrtkovci try to get protection from the authorities, from the police?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: Since I was a member of the local commune and Dobrosav Markovic was president of the Assembly of the Local Commune, we set out to Ruma together. We went to the State Security Service to see Slavko Kulundzic, who was in charge of the area, so that he would find a solution for the village because there was chaos in the village. So we went to see him, and we asked for help. This is what he said; these were his words: "Whoever has to leave, let them leave." So we didn't get any protection. As for the local police, when people asked them to help, they didn't turn them down. They just said, "Okay, okay"; and quite simply. They turned a deaf ear. They didn't intervene. They just wanted the people who were addressing them to be satisfied.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Do you know what was the goal of this harassment of the local Hrtkovci Croats by the refugees?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: Well, the goal was the ethnic cleansing, to expel the Croats so that they went to Croatia and to have the Serbs settle in Hrtkovci.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think it's a good moment for the break because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it is very timely. We'll now break for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Court is back in session. Mr. Mussemeyer, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Your Honours, before we come back to the examination-in-chief of Mr. Baricevic, we have been looking during the break for the book that Mr. Seselj mentioned. He said it would be -- the book where he said his speech was published, he said it would be called "The Major Importance of the May Elections." We found a book in the meantime that was called "The Vital Importance of the May Elections," and I would like to know from the accused if it is possible if it was this book he was talking about.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's not the title of the book. It's the title of a chapter inside the book, "The Vital Importance of the May Elections." It's a chapter in the book. Could you please show me the book, and then I will tell you everything if you have the book here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: I can do it next time. I don't have it here, but I will do it next time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please bring it in next time. That way, you can show it to us, and he will tell you that it's in the book.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, let me just tell you this: As early as in 2003, I obtained from Belgrade a complete set of all the books of my collected works in paperback. The new edition, a hard-back edition, started being put out after my arrival in The Hague, so I have 103 of the books that were published in hard-back, and I submitted to the Prosecution all that was published in paperback by 2003.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is what Mr. Seselj had told us a long time ago. When he arrived, he gave the Prosecution - not you personally - but he gave the OTP all the books in paperback. So you should have these paperback books, and in this book there is a chapter entitled "The Vital Importance of the May Elections."

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: What I can confirm is that we have the books. I was present in the courtroom when he gave us the books. It was maybe the 23rd of October, 2003, if my memory serves me correctly. But we will check it, and when we read through these books, we analysed a lot of documents, and it may be that in the near future with a Bar table motion we will try to tender parts of these books. But I will come back to the examination-in-chief of Mr. Baricevic, and Mr. Registrar, please, could we see on the monitor 65 ter number 1497. It's a press article from Vreme, and it is called "Vreme press article about murders, beatings, threats, looting, and expulsion in Hrtkovci against the non-Serb population." This article is from the 13th of July, 1992, and I would like the witness to read the paragraph -- the first paragraph, which starts with the heading "The Procedure of Moving Out." It's in the first column.

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, but I really can't see it. It's way too small for me.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judges, the first question is what this witness has to do with all that because according to his own testimony, this witness left Hrtkovci by the 15th of May, and this article was published in July of that year, 1992. So the witness cannot comment on it. I'm sure that he has never seen this at the relevant time, and this deals with things that happened after his departure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: I think we can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: We can make a decision when the witness has read about this because this article refers to events which he experienced or which he witnessed at the time. So I would like to have the witness read the paragraph which starts with: "The procedure of moving out." If he can read this, I don't know. I think we have technical problem.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'll try: "Procedure of moving out. Nedeljka, Jelica and Radmila are Serbian women, married to Croats or Hungarians. People tell them on the phone --" Well, I can't really -- could somebody else please read it? I can't read it. It's really too small. The print is too small. I can't see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, can you enlarge the left-hand page, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I have an additional objection here. The insistence on the witness reading this is nothing less than leading the witness. This witness is now made to read an article from an anti-Serb newspaper, and then he's asked to say whether he agrees with it or not. And this is not an article that deals with the time when he was there. He's supposed to come here and tell us about his experience. He's not an expert who can comment on other people's articles. And this is not an article about him so that he cannot even tell us, "Yes, this is what I stated."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you've been given this article. As far as the objection is concerned, the Trial Chamber can state this: This newspaper seems to be an anti-Serb newspaper - this is what Mr. Seselj says - and talks about what happened with those people who were present, those Serbian women who were married to Hungarians or to Croats and who were being telephoned or spoken to. It's interesting to see whether what's mentioned in this article is something which you were aware of. You have the article in front of you. Can you read this article in your own language?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can now. Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Read it out.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one remark, please. I did not leave on the 15th. I left on the 19th. The 19th, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 19th of May. Fine. Please continue to read.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Procedure of moving out. Nedeljka, Jelica and Radmila are Serb women married to Croats or Hungarians. They get telephone calls, and people shout at them in the streets, telling them that they are Ustasha whores or bad Serbs and all kinds of things. They are not the only people we talk to, and all tell a similar story. "On the 6th of May, there was a promotion rally of the Serb Radical Party. Seselj was there too. A list containing the names of 17 people was read out, people who do not belong to the village, and that's when the moving out started, willingly or by force. The latter means this: They come to your place in a group. One of them puts a paper under your nose, and you are supposed to sign it, indicating that you are willing to swap your old house where you were born for a house somewhere in Croatia. You don't even know if the house is there at all. You don't have the right to take with you your TV set, your tractor, nothing of value, least of all the money. Some 40 houses were emptied out in this manner. The rest left on their own, for the most part, after a file was put together indicating that they had been providing assistance to Croatia financially, by sending weapons, or that their sons are serving in the ZNG. Well, we almost trusted this until our turn came. Now, when they tell the same story about us, we know that this is not true. We understand that what they said about those who had gone before us was not true either. A woman says, 'My husband went'" --

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. I think this should be enough from this article, and I would like to know from you if you experienced such events and if this really -- if you can confirm this, what is written here in the newspaper.

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I can confirm the events that are described in this paper, and let me tell you what I went through. My daughter was on her way home from school, and she was stopped by some people who asked her, "Who is your father's favourite, you or your brother? Because he can take only one of you with him to Croatia, and you know what's going to happen to the other one." And then they called me on the phone. They told me, "What are you waiting for? Why don't you move out?" Not -- more than once, in fact, this happened more than once, until I agreed to swap my house.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Before we move on to the next exhibit, I would like to have this moved into evidence, this exhibit with the number 65 ter 1497.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before we give it an exhibit number: On looking at the article, I would like to turn to the end of the article where the journalist says that he met the secretary to the local Serbian Radical Party, Milan Zilic. This is what the journalist says. As far as you know, Witness, was Milan Zilic secretary to the Serbian Radical Party? This is what the journalist says.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I couldn't tell you that, really.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, can we have an exhibit number for this document, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit number P561.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, could I have on the monitor the 65 ter number 1309. It has already an exhibit number, which is 556, but I wanted to discuss this press article from "Borba" from the 14th of May, 1992, with the witness. The title is "Half of the Villagers Packing Suitcases About the Situation in Hrtkovci After Threats and Pressure By Members of the SRS Against the Non-Serb Population." Again, this is from the 14th of May, 1992, when the witness was still in the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Could you please read the second paragraph in the first column, which starts: "All troubles of the multiethnic village started ..."

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: Would you please zoom in a little bit? Is that the article you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: I don't see the beginning, the headline. I cannot say. No, I think it is not the one. It is called "Half the Village Packs Their Bags." There it is, and there's the second paragraph. I can see this now. If you could read from the beginning of the second paragraph.

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: "All the troubles of this multiethnic village started on St. George's Day when Vojislav Seselj made a speech in the center of the village clearly saying that there was no place here for the non-Serbs. From that day on, groups of unknown people have been roaming the village on a daily basis, mistreating the people, breaking into their homes and looting. Refugees from Croatia and Bosnia move by force into... " Just a moment: " ... move into the houses owned by Croats, Hungarians, or even Serbs who give them support. At the same time, as fear reigns in the village, people -- people who have to, have to. People who are --" Oh, yes, now that's better: "At the same time, as fear reigns in the village, people who pack their belongings say they have nowhere to go. Most of them have spent the last year on the frontline as JNA reservists, mostly in Vukovar. That is why they say that Croatia -- that the Croatian authorities are of no interest to them. People withdraw into their homes as dusk --"

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. Baricevic, thank you very much. I think that that is enough. What I want to know from you is if this description is correct or it corresponds to your experience or what you witnessed.

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it does correspond with this text.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judges, I think it would be only fair for the Prosecutor to ask the witness whether he agrees with the contents of the indictment; and once the witness states that he does, then there's no need for us to waste any more time. This really makes no sense at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: I would like to have the witness read, also, a second paragraph of this press article, and this is -- just a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a question before that. Witness, this newspaper, "Borba," which I'm not familiar with, this is a newspaper I assume which is published in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. It's a newspaper -- it's a daily, a Belgrade daily.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: I would have the witness to read the second paragraph after the headline: "Which Child Do You Love More."

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Do you see this, Mr. Baricevic? Do you see the headline?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Madam Usher, there is a headline which is called "Which Child Do You Love More," and I want to go to the next line --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, now it's okay. Now I see it. It's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: I want to go to the second --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Which Child Do You Love More?" "'I am from Macedonia. I'm married to a Croat man, and I've lived here for more than two decades,' says Marija Los [phoen]. 'My husband has spent three and a half months on the front in Vukovar, and we have nowhere to go, nor do we want to go anywhere.' Over the past two or three days, six houses were broken into in the village, and unknown people moved into three of them by force. The best example is Andrija Cergi. The old house where his mother used to live was given to the refugees by him, and now unknown people took away his new house. Vlado Pakic's house was broken into, as well, and unknown people broke into the house of Rozalija Cakic, an old woman, and mistreated her. Franja Samu, the sawmill manager, is also on the list of undesirables. He immediately tendered his resignation, but the workers refused to accept it. They demand that he remain at the head of the company that he managed so well. Franja Baricevic is also packing his bags. He works in the local office. At night, when he's ordered to move out over the phone, the unknown people ask him -- go as far as to ask him, 'Which child do you love more?' At the beginning of the war in Croatia" --

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. Baricevic, thank you very much. This is all I wanted you to read.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, there is a question of translation that I think it would be useful to clarify before we move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. I realised it when --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: The issue, is it three months or three days, because given the dates of the article, which appears to be the 14th of May, 1992, it is, of course, of some importance to know whether houses were invaded over "the last three months," as it says in the translation, or whether this happened over "the last three days," as indicated by the witness in his reading-out of the article. So which is it? Is it months or days?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: I don't read B/C/S, and I think it's dates -- days, but let the witness confirm it to us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Days, "over the past three days." That's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: And another issue is, there's missing a sentence, I realise now, about the sawmill --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
