utterances.text: I realise that there is missing a sentence in the English translation which deals with the sawmill director, which the witness read to us, and I can't find it in the English version which I have here, which is part of the Court binder. So this should be probably re-translated or checked for the convenience of the Chamber. It's not necessary to move this document into evidence, because it's already there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, one small question. It so happens that in the article, which I have read entirely, your name is mentioned. You are mentioned in the article. This is something which you might or might not be aware of because you work for the local authorities. During the night, you purportedly received telephone calls in which unknown people asked you which of your children you loved the most. As far as you remember, did you meet a journalist from "Borba" called Branislav Gulan?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So how could he know that you were receiving telephone calls during the night?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, this happened earlier, and people complained to each other about what was done to them. And when my daughter was intercepted, other children saw that because children went home from school together, and the children saw that my daughter was intercepted, and then they told their parents at home.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. The journalist seems to have met a lot of people because he mentioned a whole series of important figures in the village. And when he concludes, he says, "We are leaving Hrtkovci," and the village is deserted with the exception of a few people. And at the end, he says that there are some people who are going to turn to the president of the republic and the prime minister because they feel that in a federal republic, one cannot force people to leave because they are not a Serb. This is what the journalist says. As far as you know, were there citizens, sir, that seized the prime minister and the president of the republic of the situation which prevailed in that village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, let me tell you, I heard that a group of people from the village had gone to Belgrade, but I don't know who they were. This is something that I heard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So they went to Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's what I heard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did you read the papers at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, quite frankly, I didn't really feel like reading the papers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You didn't feel like it, but were the newspapers delivered to your village? Were newspapers on sale in your village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, papers were on sale regularly, every day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Mussemeyer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: In the meantime, I could find out, just to assist the honourable Judges, that this press article was also published in Mr. Seselj's book, which is called "A Scream of the Shooting Stars in 1994 in Belgrade." It's on the exhibit list and has the number 1310. So we can check, also, for the translation, maybe, that we can clarify this issue later on, just for -- to assist the Judges.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. Baricevic, the next question: We heard what happened. You read what --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that the Prosecutor must give you the complete information. This is a book of mine, that's true, but I am merely an editor. It's a compendium of all the worst attacks launched by journalists against me, and "The Scream of the Falling Stars," this title, this is a quote from Dragoslav Mihajlovic's well-known short story. His title was "The Scream of a Falling Star," and I paraphrased it ironically, saying -- calling it "The Scream of the Falling Stars" because I wanted to have all the journalists attacks against me and the Serb Radical Party put in one place.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. Baricevic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. For the transcript, we need to put the following conclusion down: This article, P555, was published in Mr. Seselj's book. In this book, there is a collection of all articles that were written either against him or against his party, and this article is in this book.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, it was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: It was the Exhibit P556 instead of P555.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely. You're right, and the Registrar also told me that it was, indeed, the P556. Thank you. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. Baricevic, what was your reaction after these events happened?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: When I started receiving those threats, particularly those against my children, I packed them up one night and sent them to Croatia via Hungary. They went to my wife's parents'. I sent my wife and my children there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Did you remain in Hrtkovci at that time?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I remained there for a couple of days, and I continued working as usual. But three days later, a man came, a man from Jaksic. He went into Ante Grizelj's house in Hrtkovci. He took the house, and he gave me an address telling me where my new house was to be. It was in Pavla Radica Street, number 7, in Jaksic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Did you see the house before you went there? Sorry, the question was not very correct. Did you sign a contract to get the owner -- to become the owner of this house?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: I signed a contract in Pozega, in an office of an attorney-at-law in Pozega. Mira Primorac was her name. Well, what else could I do? You have to take what was an offer. I left two houses behind, and all I got was a house that was damaged, burnt down. But I got out alive, and my children were safe.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Could you please describe how your house was in Hrtkovci and how your house was in the village where you had to move later on?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: Well, the house in the village of Jaksic had been burned down, while my house in Hrtkovci was built in 1983 with solid brick. It was 12 by 11 metres. That was the surface area. It was my house, while our family house was in the same yard. The family house was built in 1953, and it was in a very good condition. And I forgot to mention that my house also had an attic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: So you exchanged two houses for one house?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, I would like to have the 65 ter number 1976 on the monitor, and I would like to go on page 162 of the B/C/S version, the Serbian version.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: And, Mr. Baricevic, could you then please read the first three paragraphs which follow a very long question on that page. I can see the question, which is in bold, and I would like you to read after the question the first three paragraphs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Prosecutor, could you tell us exactly where this article comes from?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Sorry. I forgot to give you this important information. It's a chapter of Mr. Seselj's book of interviews. It's called "Philippics of a Chetnik Duke." This is one of the 80 books which Mr. Seselj provided to the Prosecution on the 29th of October, 2003.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: And Mr. Baricevic, just to repeat, could you please read us the first three paragraphs? It's Mr. Seselj's answer to a long question from the journalist.

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: It says: "I categorically claim, with full moral and material responsibility, that there have never been national persecutions, so-called ethnic cleansings, under the auspices or in the organisation of the Serb Radical Party, never took place in the organisation of the Serb Radical Party, or will that ever be the case. Paid witnesses who accuse us as assigned cannot -- or can they have any evidence against us. Let them give the names, the locations and dates of places where Serb Radicals abused someone, persecuted someone, or killed someone just because they were not of Serb ethnicity."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "In the famous ..."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "In the famous ..."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The best thing would be for me to read this to the witness. Obviously, he can't read very well; and therefore, he violates my text, Judges.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you're having a difficult time reading this text?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I can't really see it right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we zoom in, maybe? The Registrar is telling me that it cannot be made any bigger. The text cannot be made any bigger, unfortunately. If you can't read any more, it's okay. Mr. Prosecutor, could you please ask a question from the quoting of the text, and maybe he will say "yes" or "no" or "I don't know."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have an objection. Because the Prosecutor asked for this section to be read, then I do insist that all of it be read out because if the witness paused right now when the most important thing was supposed to be read out, then the public will be denied the most important part. It has to do with my statement, my speech, my answer to the journalist's question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: I have a hard-copy version that maybe we can try with it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that in such situations, even the court officer who speaks the Serbian language can read it out. Why make a witness read when it's hard for him to read?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you have the text in hard copy. Can you read it? If you can't read it, tell me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot. I cannot read it. The print is very small.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let me ask my fellow Judges whether Mr. Seselj should read it out loud.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The best solution would be for the interpreters to read the text, since it's on the screen, and they could site-translate it. Is it possible?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Someone has to read out the text in the original for the interpreters to be able to interpret. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Obviously, it's too tall an order for anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: We might give a hard copy to the interpreters if it's easier for them to read.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Usher, could you please get the hard copy from the OTP and bring it to the interpreter's booth, French and English.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hope that means that the text will be read out in Serbian and will then be interpreted into your language, Judges.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters note that according to the Rules, someone in the courtroom should read out the text, and then the booths can interpret it into the respective languages. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the interpreter read it in Serbian, and the French and English interpreters will then translate it. It seems to be very difficult.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, it seems that it is impossible. Well, Mr. Prosecutor, you should have thought of it earlier. During the proofing session, you should have checked your witness's glasses. Obviously, this is an impossibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: We did this, and he could read because the light was better.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's nothing we can do now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, now the interpreters have a copy of this text. If I read it, then they can check whether I'm reading it right, and then they can tell you because I assume that before you did not trust me to read it properly, but now you do have someone who can do the check for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since the interpreters have the hard copy, please read the excerpt in your own language, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm reading after the witness read it, right? "In the famous Hrtkovci blown out of proportion in the media that have been portrayed as crown evidence of our alleged tortures, there were no killings on ethnic grounds. There was a killing out of avarice. It so happened that the victim was a Croat, but the killers were apprehended and will be held responsible. It is true that some people did move out of the village, but Croats did it of their own free will. No one forced them to do that, let alone members of our party. Of their own free will, voluntarily, they exchanged properties and houses with Serbs from Croatia, and in these transactions, in the organisation of the Catholic Church, usually they fared better. However, Hrtkovci continues to be used as proof," quote/unquote --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Prosecutor, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: I only wanted to have the witness read the paragraph which Mr. Seselj finished some sentences ago, not the next one. That was my intention. If he wants to continue, it's not -- I wouldn't object.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think these two sentences at the end are very important, but then whatever you decide.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Read those two sentences.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "However, Hrtkovci continues to be used as proof" - and "proof" is under quotation marks - "that even in the territory of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, there was ethnic cleansing. This is contributed to by many of our traitors who are wandering around the world politically prostituting themselves and lying in accordance with the orders issued by their wealthy masters, the builders of a new world order."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Seselj, for having read this out. Mr. Prosecutor, could you please put your question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. Baricevic, was it your experience -- is it correct what Mr. Seselj said in this article, that no Croats have been forced to leave Hrtkovci, especially not from SRS members?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: That is not the absolute truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, you are one of the -- you were one of the witnesses who actually signed an exchange of houses. You told us that you had a brick house, another house that had been built in 1953, so your personal case is very interesting for us because you signed the contract at an attorney-at-law, Ms. Primorac. How did you manage to go to this attorney-at-law? Did you go on your own volition, or did someone tell you, "Go see Primorac"? Tell us exactly how this happened.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry. The house was a newly-built one in 1983, in 1983. The old one was built in 1953. As for this house, for which I got the address, and I went to that address, actually --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Who gave you this address, Primorac's address?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've already mentioned that Spasojevic came to Grizelj's house. Spasojevic was from Jaksic, and he immediately chose the house and gave me an address for Branko Milosavljevic, and I exchanged houses with him because that is what was said at the rally, that Croats would get addresses of Serbs from Croatia. I got this address, and I went there after I had already transferred my wife and children to Croatia. So you take whatever you can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is not extremely clear. A person called Spasojevic came to Grizelj's house, and Spasojevic came from Jaksic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And he gave you the address of Branko Milosavljevic's house, who is the person that you were going to exchange houses with; is that it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, precisely, because they were neighbours. Their houses were about 150 metres away from each other.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you hadn't wanted to do this, could you have said, "I'm not interested, I'd rather stay here"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were all sorts of threats and tortures every day. I had already moved my children out so that they could stay alive, my wife, too. I had to choose the best option out of many bad ones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Then you go to the attorney-at-law, Primorac, to sign the contract. Who gave you the address of this attorney? Who told you to go see Primorac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, I addressed the owner of the house, Branko Milosavljevic. Then we went to see the lawyer, the attorney.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. And the lawyer prepared all the papers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They had already prepared all the documentation. I took what they gave me so that I could live in peace.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The new house that you obtained, was it better or worse than the house you had before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am sorry. We don't seem to be understanding each other. That house had been old and torched.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You lost in this deal. You had a good house, and you obtained a burnt, old house. You were tricked?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I lost my house that had been totally new. For the building of a house, you need two generations to be involved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I understand now. Mr. Prosecutor, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. Baricevic, do you know if the Catholic Church was involved in this exchange of property?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, the Catholic Church did not take part in the exchange of properties in any way. People, Catholics, went to get certificates of baptism and of marriages to prove that they are Croat Catholics in order to regulate their papers and documentation for the future, in terms of future documents, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. Baricevic, one last question. At the beginning of your testimony, you told us that about 75 per cent of the inhabitants of Hrtkovci were Croats. Do you know the percentage of Croats who live today in Hrtkovci?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know what the percentage is, but I do know that 460 households moved out of Hrtkovci. I know that within one month's time after the rally, 300 households had moved out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Baricevic. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One follow-up question after this last question by the Prosecutor. Let me come back to this article by Branislav Gulan in "Borba." In this article - you'll have to look at it; you can trust me - he says that there are 20 different ethnicities in this village. This was a very composite village, and he says that were 1.079 Croats, 558 Serbs, 516 Hungarians, 452 Yugoslavs, 4 Macedonians, and some Slovaks, Russians, Albanians, Montenegrins and Romas. When looking at all these figures, we note that the Serbs are in a minority, 558 Serbs. Maybe there were Serbs among the Yugoslavs, so the figure for Serbs might be a bit higher, but Croats and Hungarians were in a majority. Now, after all these flats were exchanged, should we understand that the majority of Croats had left?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, most Croats had moved out of Hrtkovci.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. You were a victim in this house exchange because you obtained an old, burnt house and whereas to build a nice house it takes at least two generations. And your own house had been built in the 1980s. So you'd been had in this exchange; you lost. Now, eventually, did you get any compensation, or did you lose everything?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I never got any compensation. The only thing I managed to do was, with the assistance of two witnesses or two guarantors, rather, to get a small loan to build up the house.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. That's all. So you were swindled. You lost in this exchange, obviously. Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: I would like to move the last article from Mr. Seselj's book where we read from into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Let's give it a number. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, please, it is very important for the Prosecutor to say what year this book was published.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The article published in Mr. Seselj's book, could you tell us exactly, what is the date for this article?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: According to my information, the date is 1994, and it was published in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1994, Belgrade. Very well. My fellow Judge has a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, do you know anything about the murder of Milan Stefanac, or did this happen after you had left? Do you know anything about this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I heard about this. It happened after I had left. I heard about the killing of Milan Stefanac and that he was found in the neighbouring village. I don't know about the details. I don't know anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter number 01976 will be Exhibit number P562.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It would probably be good to have the break right now. We will resume around 20 to 6.00, and Mr. Seselj can then start his cross-examination. It's best to proceed this way. Let's break for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Court is back in session. Mr. Seselj, you have the floor for your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Baricevic, when you came to Slavonska Pozega in May 1992 and later on, did you talk at all with the Croatian police or any other state services of the Croatian state?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: When I came to Croatia, I went to get the papers, the ID papers, and I don't see what you're driving at when you talk about interviews or talks.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, you can't really see that. You're not supposed to see that. You're supposed to answer my question.

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: No, I have not talked to anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So you did not talk to anyone, to the secret service or any other state organs?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: In the 16 years, you never gave any statements about what happened to you in Hrtkovci, as you allege, to any of the Croatian authorities? That's what I mean.

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: Well, that's not the secret police.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: What is it, then?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: That's the court.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Which court?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: The Military Prosecutor's Office in Osijek.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And when did you give a statement to them?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: I can't recall the exact date, but it was sometime in 1994, let's say.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And what did you say in that statement of yours?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: The same things that I stated here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Everything?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And what did the Military Prosecutor's Office in Osijek actually do? What was it that they were investigating?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, how come, then, that they summoned you in 1994? Did you go to Osijek from Slavonska Pozega?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: No, they came to my place.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: To Slavonska Pozega? To Jaksic, which is a suburb of Slavonska Pozega?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Who came to see you?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: How many people came to see you?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: Two.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Were they in uniform?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So they were in plain clothes. What did they tell you, then?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: They asked me the same questions that the Prosecutor asked me now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: About everything that allegedly happened to you in Hrtkovci; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And did they put together a statement on the basis of that interview? Did they tape the interview?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I didn't see them make any recordings.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But did they put together a statement that you signed?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did they just take notes, then?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: Well, they did write down something, but I don't know what that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did you have any other interviews with any other state organs?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So that was the only one?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: Not with the Croatian state organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And how did you get in contact with the OTP?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: Well, they came to see me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: To Slavonska Pozega?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: What did they tell you?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: They asked me how I -- what the situation was like down there, and I told them the same thing that I told you now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: What year was that?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: Well, that was five or six years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: How many times did you talk to the investigators from The Hague?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. Just a few.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: What does it mean, "just a few"? One, two?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: Two, two.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: In what year?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: Last year.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did you sign any statements last year?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judges, I did not receive the statement that this witness provided to the investigators of the OTP last year. I think that this is such a major issue that it actually renders my cross-examination pointless. I only have the statement that he gave in the year 2002.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's try and understand what this is about. Witness, we don't have it. Last year, did you give the OTP a new statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. That's the only statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you answered Mr. Seselj, you said, "Yes." Mr. Seselj asked you whether there was one or two, and you said, "Two." And Mr. Seselj said, "In what year?" And you said, "Last year."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One statement was given to the Tribunal in The Hague, and the people who came from Osijek, that was the Military Prosecutor's Office. They came to see me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's a statement which you've signed, since we have it, dated 28th of September, 2002, given to the Prosecution. Was there another statement, or wasn't there one made here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's the only one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: What happened last year, then?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: Last year, an investigator came to see me, but it was just to talk to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And what did he want from you in this conversation?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: To confirm the statement that I had given.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And did you confirm it?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did you sign anything at that time?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: How could you then confirm it? Orally?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I read the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But did you sign it once you'd read it?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: Well, it had already been signed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Judge, you can see that I am right. The Prosecution has to have a record of this interview or conversation that took place last year. There has to be a note or a record of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you had this conversation last year with the investigator, did he give you his name? Who was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Paulo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He's Italian?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He showed you something. Did he make you sign something or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, he did not ask anything of the sort. He just gave me the statement to read. It had been translated into Croatian, so I was to read it. I didn't sign anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You read the 2002 statement, the only statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The only statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mussemeyer or Ms. Dahl, the investigator, Paolo Stocchi, did he prepare a report, or was it unofficial?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: I'm not aware that he prepared a report. I'm pretty sure that he did this, but if I may help to find out of this confusion. According to my records, there exists one statement the witness gave. You mentioned it already, on the 27th or 28th of September, 2002. And we have a 92 bis package where the witness signed more or less again the same statement that is dated the 1st of December, 2005. It's a 92 ter -- 92 bis package, and let me -- it's in -- completely in the Serbian or Croatian language, and it was given before the presiding officer, Marco Bonavello [phoen] on the 1st of December, 2005.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This 92 bis statement was for which trial ?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Let me check this. I have it here. I guess it's for the trial against Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In other words, you had contemplated using a 92 bis statement. Mr. Seselj, you've got your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, Mr. Mussemeyer now said that this statement from 2005 is more or less the same as the 2002 statement. I'm interested in both more and in less. I'm not interested in the same at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If there is a 2005 statement, Mr. Seselj should be made aware of it, more or less. If it's more, then it is against him. Otherwise, it's exculpatory. Whatever the case may be, he should have been given the statement. What happened, again?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: I cannot tell you at the moment if it hasn't been disclosed. I'm pretty sure that it has. I can read what is said here, that: "The attached statement, dated the 27th-28th of September, 2002, and certified by the undersigned on 1st December, 2005, the said witness is identified as the author." This is the normal 92 bis procedure which was done at that time before the Rules changed, but I will check if this has been disclosed to Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Please proceed, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Baricevic, did you talk to the investigators in The Hague in 1995?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: In 1995, well, I can't really remember what time it was, but as far as statements are concerned, I only gave one statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: When you say "Rujan," that's the Croatian term for "September"?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: Well, "September."

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So the term "Rujan," what month would that be?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment. Perhaps the Prosecutor has something to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: I found the disclosure date of this 92 bis package. It's the ERN number 0465-6571 to 6580, and that was disclosed to Mr. Seselj on the 10th of July, 2006. And the receipt was number 23, and I think Mr. Seselj signed it. I have to check this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, it seems that this has been disclosed to you on the 10th of July, 2006. The receipt number is number 23.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I received this disclosure, the 2002 statement, twice. It was retyped in the meantime, but there is the same year indicated on both, 2002. There is no mention of 2005 or 2006. And now the Prosecution has to prove that it disclosed this to me. So I do have two statements. The text is identical. Different typewriters, but the same date, the 27th and the 28th of September, 2002.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Mr. Baricevic, I asked you whether in 1995 you provided any statements to the investigators from The Hague.

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I've already replied. I can't recall what the year was, but that was the only statement that I gave to the investigators of the Tribunal in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I have a document from the Prosecution. The number is 0307-3665, where it says that a translator of the OTP confirms that on the 28th of September, 1995, that she interpreted a conversation, an interview with you. The date is 1995, yet I never received any statement -- any record of it. But I do have this document that was disclosed by mistake to me. Let me repeat the number if you want me to. So it's 1995, an interview was conducted with you. I have only one piece of written evidence to prove it. It is a confirmation, a certificate by the interpreter, indicating that she interpreted that interview for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, don't you think there might be a mistake as far as the date is concerned? The 28th of September, 1995, or the 28th of September, 2002? Maybe it's one and the same thing. Witness, you must tell the truth. Mr. Seselj is working a lot, sees all the details, and nothing escapes him. He has a document before him. He gives us ERN number 0307-3665, which seems to indicate that the interpreter from the OTP purportedly said something concerning one Croatian word, "ulan." I'm not quite sure what it is. So my question is very simple. In 1995, i.e., a very short time after the events which took place in 1992, did you meet an investigator from the OTP, or did you only meet him in 2002?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I met up with the investigators, and when I made my statement, that was the only statement that I ever gave to investigators, just this one statement. I can't remember dates now, when it was that this actually happened, but it was only one statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Mussemeyer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: This investigator certification which the accused is referring to belongs to the 92 bis package from 2005. It has the same ERN number, 0307 and then 3665, which the accused was quoting from. There must be a mistake on the date. It's, in fact -- it says the 28th of -- I don't know the English name of the month, but from -- September 1995. But what the accused omitted is that there is a second ERN number on the same page, which has the number 0465-6579, and it contains the 92 bis package from December. So there is a mistake in the date, but in fact it has been disclosed, and it's also proof that this 92 ter -- 92 bis package has been disclosed to Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you for this clarification. Witness, you only saw the investigators for your statement in 2002 and not in 1995. Mr. Seselj, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But, Mr. President, he saw Paolo Pastore-Stocchi in 2005, as well, or last year as he said a few moments ago; the witness, I mean. What remains unclear is what happened in 1995. If this is a mistake and if an OTP typist can make that kind of a mistake, instead of typing out "2002," type out "1995," then I really don't know what kind of psychologist could explain that kind of error, or typing "2005" instead of "2002" or "2008." However, that might be possible. However, if somebody lives in 2002 and types out "1995," that's a mistake that's impossible, or perhaps it may happen. Maybe there's some new diseases that came up in the world now. I've been in prison for a long time, so perhaps there is these new illnesses that have cropped up behind the prison walls.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the time being, the Prosecution is saying that it must be a typo. "1995" was typed in instead of "2002." That is the explanation provided by the Prosecution. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: When you talked to these investigators from The Hague in 2002, you talked to Paolo Pastore-Stocchi; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: I did talk to him, but I don't know what the year was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did you talk to him both times or only once?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: I talked to him twice. However, I don't remember dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. You talked to him twice?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And you say to him that at the rally in Hrtkovci, I asked for all children from mixed marriages to be killed, right?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You said that to him?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And when you said that to him, what was his reaction? I'm really interested in that. Was he surprised?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know whether he was surprised, but that's the way it was written down.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did he just listen to you calmly and then write -- and then he wrote up this statement, and you signed it without a comment of any kind?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I signed the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Without him asking you anything in relation to that?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: Well, we talked. I don't know about the details. I don't know about individual details.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. If you don't know, you don't know. I can understand that as age advances, people start losing their memory and various processes start in people's heads, but when did you come to The Hague to testify now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment. A follow-up question. The question put to you by Mr. Seselj is extremely important. On the 27th and 28th of September, 2002, you meet the investigator of the OTP, and you talk to him, and the conversation lasts for how long? How many hours? Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We met twice, two days, eight or nine hours both times.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you told him a lot of things, and then he prepared your statement, which you signed and which was read back to you in your language. This is what is written in the document. When you talked to the investigator, did you tell him, "I remember that Mr. Seselj in his speech said that children born from mixed marriages should be killed," and he said that again, or you said that Mr. Seselj talked about mixed marriages, and you didn't say that the children should be killed? What did you tell the investigator, precisely?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I would like to repeat what it was that I had said. He had said that mixed marriages should be divorced and that the children should be killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj said that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's what I heard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And you said that to the investigator, who translated that. Please proceed, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: When did you come here to The Hague to testify in these proceedings?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: I came on Sunday.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: It's Tuesday today, right? So you've been here for two days?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: How many conversations did you have with the representatives of the OTP over those two days?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: One.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did you go through your entire statement?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: When you came to this section where you claim that I had stated at the rally that all children from mixed marriages should be killed, did the representative of the OTP caution you that you should perhaps give this some thought, whether that is what actually happened?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: They asked me whether you said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And you confirmed?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And then they kept silent about it?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: They said, "Well, if that's the way it is, then let's move on."

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So that was this very brief conversation that you had, and that's how it ended?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that the tensions in Hrtkovci started at the time of Milosevic's rallies in the 1980s, right?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: What you call Milosevic's rallies were actually the rallies of the Kosovo Serbs, right?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know whose they were, these rallies, but these rallies were held from Kosovo to Vojvodina. They were Milosevic's.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Says who?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: Well, that's what people said, that they were Milosevic's rallies.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Were these rallies that were led by people from Kosovo, like Kosta Bulatovic, Miroslav Solevic, and many others, Milorad Albijanic and so on? I can't even remember them all now.

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I didn't say -- well, I've already said that I did not deal in politics, and I really couldn't say who it was that was in charge of these rallies.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did Kosovo Serbs consider themselves highly jeopardised by the Albanian separatists?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I was not in Kosovo, and I wouldn't really -- I mean, well, I wouldn't comment on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: What's the reason for you to be so restless about these rallies? Did anybody mention Croats at these rallies?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: I stated clearly that individuals at the time -- well, I mean, let me put this in a simpler way. Their heads were raised.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: What individuals?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: Individuals in the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: How did they raise their heads?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: Well, they wore Chetnik caps, and they shouted, "This is Serbia, this is not Croatia," things like that. As I said, these small provocations started.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Why were you bothered by the Chetnik caps? These are traditional Serbian caps, traditional Serbian insignia, the Serb coat of arms.

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I said that this was a calm, peaceful village of hardworking people who were not interested in politics. They were only interested in working and working yet again.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: If somebody chants, "Serbia, Serbia," or, "This is Serbia," why does that bother you? Hrtkovci has always been Serbia, right?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: Well, nothing bothers me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Why would somebody say, "This is not Croatia" when everybody knew that it was not Serbia and Srem could certainly not be Croatia in any way?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I did not say that it was Croatia or that it was Serbia. I minded my own business, and I worked honestly in that village where I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I'm not interested in what it was that you were doing. How come you made this statement - that's what I'm interested in - that the tensions started from Milosevic's rallies? And you are not in a position to state that to me, and you did state that. How come?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I've explained that these were individuals and that they started a bit --

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: What?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: Well, a bit of unrest in the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: What kind of unrest?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I've already explained that some people, I mean -- well, wore caps and sang songs, and that is what caused unrest among the people.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Why would songs bother you or cause unrest? Were Croats referred to in these songs?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know if they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So why would that disturb you, Serb patriotic songs? Why would that disturb you?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. I don't know whether these Serb songs were patriotic or whatever, but I said once, and I repeat again, that that is when unrest started.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But you cannot explain to me what kind of unrest this was. How was that reflected?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I've told you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Somebody sang a song or wore a Serb coat of arms on his cockade?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So what's strange about that, and what is disturbing about that? We are ridding ourselves of communism. We are renewing old Serb traditions. Are you sorry that we've rid ourselves of communism? And you did not leave the League of Communists in 1980 when Tito died. It was only in 1990 when the League of Communists fell apart, right?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: No, no, when Tito died.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Who did you return your membership card to?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: I left it at the premises of the local commune.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: What does the local commune have to do with the League of Communists?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: The party secretary came there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Why did you go on paying membership fees?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: But the records say that you did. Well, all right. You say in your statement, the one that you signed, that in 1990 the Serbian Renewal Movement and the Serb Radical Party, led by Vuk Draskovic, or rather, Vojislav Seselj, opened their branches in Hrtkovci. That is on page 2 of your statement, paragraph 4?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: How come in 1990 when the Serb Radical Party did not even exist then?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: I know that people were signing up. I don't know if it existed or not, but people were signing up.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: How can people sign up into a party that doesn't exist?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: It is possible, but it's hard to explain, right?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: No, no. You should ask them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Who is "them"?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: These members.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: How can I ask them when they did not exist in 1990, when it did not exist at the time, and you claim that they signed up then and that the Serb Radical Party opened its branch in Hrtkovci, and the Serb Radical Party was established on the 23rd of February, 1991? You claim that a year before that, it had its branch in Hrtkovci and the people were signing up?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: Well, perhaps I got the date wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: All right. Maybe you got the date wrong, but you have been making way too many mistakes. You say that Ostoja Sibincic was president of the local SPO and Aleksa Ejic, president of the local branch of the Serb Radical Party, right?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Aleksa Ejic was never a member of the Serb Radical Party.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mussemeyer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Your Honours, we gave or disclosed to Mr. Seselj proofing notes where we were correcting this. When Mr. Baricevic was proofed, he realised this mistake, and this has been disclosed to Mr. Seselj last week. So he shouldn't insist on this. He knows that he has corrected himself and shouldn't try to confuse the witness. He knows about this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Seselj, the Prosecutor told you that the witness had made -- had confused things.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Mr. President, what should I care about what the Prosecutor notified me or not? I am trying to find chinks in the armour in the testimony of this witness here and in his previous statement. And as far as the information about the proofing session is concerned, that's not something that I can rely on. Of course, I can rely on it if there are any weaknesses there, but now the fact that the Prosecutor is trying to fix the mistakes that the witness has made, that's of no concern to me. You can see that the witness was wrong about the year when the SRS was formed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was a mistake, and the witness has recognised it. However, you were putting a very important question on Ostoja Sibincic, so please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: How can you say that Aleksa Ejic was the president of the local branch of the Serb Radical Party when he never was a member of the Serb Radical Party? The whole of Hrtkovci knows that, and Aleksa Ejic confirmed that when he came here to testify before you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: It's, again, the same. This has been corrected in the proofing notes. It has been disclosed to Mr. Seselj. If you want to, I can read what has been clarified, and I think Mr. Seselj shouldn't use this any longer because it's not correct.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, this is not the way that the witness's statement can be corrected. The witness confirmed now that Aleksa Ejic was the president of the Serbian Radical Party. He confirmed that here and now in front of you, and it is obvious that this witness was turned into a tool, but he is unable to fulfill his task, to accomplish his task. And please do not allow the Prosecutor to interrupt my cross-examination in this manner because the witness confirmed here in front of all that Aleksa Ejic was the president of the local branch of the Serbian Radical Party.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mussemeyer, I thought I understand, when you started your -- the beginning of the in-chief, that Mr. Aleksa Ejic had these political functions, but obviously it seems that during the proofing, he was also wrong? He also made a mistake?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: What I can read to you -- the proofing notes are very short. It says --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Please proceed. Do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: The ICTY statement, page 2, submitted on 27th and 28th September, 2002. Baricevic stated that Aco Ejic was the president of the SRS branch in Hrtkovci. During the proofing, Baricevic stated that Ejic was the president of the local SPO --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Counsel is kindly asked to slow down when reading.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Excuse me. "During the proofing, Baricevic stated that Ejic was the president of the local SPO party of Vuk Draskovic. In this respect, during the proofing, Baricevic said that what he said in the ICTY statement about Ejic being president of the SRS in Hrtkovci was a mistake. Baricevic confirmed that there was no SRS office in Hrtkovci, at least until Baricevic left Hrtkovci." And there's a second paragraph. It says: "During the proofing, Baricevic stated that Ostoja Sibincic was working together with the Radicals in Hrtkovci. In the ICTY statement, page 2, Baricevic stated that in 1991, Sibincic was an active member of the SRS. Baricevic does not actually know --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Counsel is kindly asked to slow down for interpretation.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judges, will I be cross-examining Mr. Mussemeyer as the representative of the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please let Mr. Mussemeyer finish reading this note that he sent to you. I had no knowledge of it, so please continue. There was -- what was it after "Baricevic does not know"?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: "Baricevic does not actually know whether Sibincic was officially a member of the SRS or whether he was only hanging around with SRS sympathizers." These are the proofing notes which we have disclosed to the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. It was important to know this. Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is much more important to note that today, in his examination-in-chief, this witness here in front of you, you had that in the transcript, stated that Aleksa Ejic founded the Serbian Radical Party and that Ostoja Sibincic founded the Serbian Renewal Movement in Hrtkovci. You can see that in his examination-in-chief. Please, refer yourselves to the transcript. What do I care what it says in the proofing session notes prepared by the Prosecution? The witness confirmed today in the courtroom that Aleksa Ejic founded the Serbian Radical Party in Hrtkovci. And as for what is written there, well, the Prosecution was amazed when they realised whom they brought here to testify, and that is why now they're showing this information based on the proofing notes. I'm not interested in that. I'm interested in what the witness said in the examination-in-chief where he said, and then he confirmed it on cross, that Aleksa Ejic founded the Serbian Radical Party in Hrtkovci. That's what the witness said in the examination-in-chief and on cross, and now the Prosecution is trying to correct the witness. Well, this really cannot be. This is impermissible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Witness, in the examination-in-chief, you said that Aleksa Ejic had created the Serbian Radical Party in Hrtkovci. I remember that. It now seems that you had corrected this during the proofing session. So why is it that when you answered Mr. Mussemeyer's question early this afternoon, you said something that you had corrected earlier? I can't reconcile this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I may have been wrong, but I always thought that Ostoja Sibincic was a member of the Serbian Radical Party. I did mention Aco Ejic here once, but I kept saying that Ostoja was a member of the Radical Party.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I have two questions for you. I would like to know whether Mr. Aleksa Ejic set up the Serbian Radical Party in your village.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, for a time he was the president, but later on he withdrew. Since his wife was Hungarian, he realised that no good could come out of this, and that's why he withdrew. He was not active.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A second question, now. Ostoja Sibincic, was he a member of the Serbian Radical Party?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He says that he was a member. I did not see his membership card.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judges, the witness again denied what is contained in the proofing notes. He repeated once again. When you, Mr. President, asked him, he confirmed that Aleksa Ejic was the president of the Serbian Radical Party in Hrtkovci, so the information contained in the proofing notes is a forgery. It's a fabrication. It misrepresents what the witness stated here in a courtroom in the examination-in-chief, on cross, and in response to the Judges' questions. So now we can see what the Prosecution is doing in the proofing sessions, what it makes use of. Should I continue, then?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You said that as early as in 1991, a group of 160 refugees had come from Slavonia and that it engendered tensions in Hrtkovci; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, 160 refugees came.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And you said that the local commune provided housing for the refugees, and that provided them with stoves, food, things of that nature?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Where did the local commune find housing for them?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: In the various houses. If somebody had two houses, if somebody's parents died, then they were put in older houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: In the houses where nobody lived?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, for a while.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And you also provided them with houses of people who had not lived in Hrtkovci for a long time, but they gave their approval for their houses to be used in this manner? You spoke to them on the phone, and they gave their approval?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: I think there was only one such house.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, there were several, but you don't have to recall every single detail. It is important for me to confirm that this kind of thing happened. And then the refugees who started to move into the empty houses started entering some of the empty houses without asking anyone because they didn't want to keep their wives, their children out in the rain; they needed to find a roof to put over their heads?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: Well, they moved in by force. They broke into houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Into empty houses?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: No, not into empty houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, they were furnished?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, furnished, appliances.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: They were empty in terms of the inhabitants? Nobody lived in them. That's what I meant. Is that so? But what do you mean if -- what do you think, if somebody flees from Croatia because he's faced with threats that his family would be killed, and this person comes to Serbia with his wife and children, and he sees an empty house, nobody had lived there for years; do you think that this person would really care about laws and would not move into this house but would rather keep the wife and the children in the forest somewhere? What's more logical than for such a person to get into an empty apartment or house and to live there until he is expelled?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You don't think so. You stated here that Sibincic transferred in late 1991 to the Serbian Radical Party, and when the Judges asked you, you said that in May 1992, you don't know whether he was formally a member of the Serbian Radical Party; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: No, that's not so.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: It is so.

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: I said that I never saw his membership card.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So how did you know that he joined the Serbian Radical Party at all?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: Well, how did I know? I knew because the people talked that the Radicals -- that they are Radicals and that he was their chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: The chief of the Radicals. And what happened with Milan Zilic, the Radical who founded the party in Hrtkovci? He was the chairman of the local board.

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: So although there was a living president of the Serbian Radical Party, Milan Zilic, you invent some other presidents?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: I know that all the dirty work was done by Ostoja Sibincic and that he represented himself as the president of the Radical Party.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, we know that you were a member of the League of Communists. We know that you also had some municipal duties for some while, for some time. You seem to be a person that is able to understand things. If what you're saying is true, if it is true that Mr. Ostoja Sibincic was the president of the Serbian Radical Party in Hrtkovci, then Mr. Seselj comes to deliver his speech on May 6th; he should be on the stage to say, "Brothers and sisters of Serbia, let me introduce Mr. Seselj, who's going to speak to you," but it is Ilic instead that takes the floor to introduce Seselj. How can you explain that? How can you explain that the president of the Serbian Radical Party is not on the stage when Mr. Seselj is coming, and there are two people that are there to prepare for his entrance, you know, Mr. Zilic and this lady, Mr. Seselj being the third, and we have no mention of Sibincic at all on stage? Do you find this normal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, well, I don't know. The only thing that I do know is that Ostoja Sibincic was in charge of the people. He gave them the addresses. He led the Radicals. Now, as to the actual functions, who was the secretary, who was the treasurer, who was really in charge, I don't know that because I was not a member of that party. But the one thing that I know is I know the people who instructed other people to cause this kind of misery in the village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Well, in 1991, did the Serb refugees from Croatia come only to Hrtkovci, or did they go all over Serbia, especially in Vojvodina?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: I know only about Hrtkovci.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: You didn't leave Hrtkovci at all?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Uh-huh. So it is your impression that the Serb refugees came only to Hrtkovci; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know whether they went to other villages. I don't know the figures, but I do know what happened in Hrtkovci.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did you say that up until April 1992 -- please focus. April 1992, that by that time there were already 500 refugees in Hrtkovci?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And the problems were really great?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: It was impossible to house all those refugees; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: The second wave of refugees, when they came, the local commune again responded to the situation and provided temporary accommodation for those people in the property of where there were beds and a kitchen and bathrooms.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I would like to quote back to you what you said, that the problems became very great.

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And the refugees became very unhappy?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, because they had been promised houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Who promised them houses?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: I guess the Serb authorities in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: What Serb authorities in Croatia? How could they promise them houses in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: Well, where the war was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: I guess there were the Croatian authorities there, the ones that expelled them. Why would the Serb authorities expel them? There were Serb authorities in the Serbian Krajina, in Western Slavonia in this case.

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: Well, they came from Western Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Yes, but Grubisno Polje was in Croat hands, and then in December 1991, Croats took most of Western Slavonia, and Serbs had only Okocani and a small section of Topokrac [phoen], so it was the Croatian authorities that expelled them; is that so?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know who promised them houses. All I said was that those people had been duped, and I'm sure that Serbs did promise them that. They told them, "Go there. There are empty houses there because people left to join the Ustashas, the Ustasha army."

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Yes, yes, sure. Serbs expelled Serbs just to spite you. This is quite clear. Now, the refugees want the problems to be solved. That's in April, and you claim that they wanted me to attend the meeting of the local commune where their problems would be discussed?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: No, that's not what I said. I said that they wanted to meet with Vojislav Seselj, not of the local commune, but for Vojislav Seselj to meet with them to solve those issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: With the refugees?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, only with the refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: And what kind of an act or what kind of a player I was at that time to be able to solve that problem?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Did I -- was I in power at that time?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: How many deputies did the SRS have in the Assembly?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Only one. Does this refresh your memory? Well, you don't know that. You only know what was written to you, that you have to repeat like a parrot all the time, and the moment we diverge from that, you start to sweat.

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know anything. I don't know anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, just think about the following situation: Did you know anything about the political situation in Serbia, or is it that in your village you just didn't care about what was happening elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not really follow political developments. I minded my own business. I know what happened in the village. Now, as for the politics, that's not something that I followed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When very unhappy refugees call on Mr. Seselj, who could have been their saviour, the person who was going to solve all their problems, at the time Mr. Seselj had a political party that had one representative, one member of Parliament. So when it seems that he didn't even agree with Mr. Milosevic on a good number of subjects, how was he supposed to solve this huge problem, this huge Serbian problem that was of great amplitude? Did you think about this, or did just no one think about it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you see, I don't know what was going on in people's heads, but they demanded that Vojislav Seselj come and solve their problems. I said that the first time they made this demand, a woman came from Ruma and she met with them. They were unhappy, and then they demanded yet again that he should come, and I guess that a meeting was arranged with Seselj, and he came to Hrtkovci on the 6th of May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One last question. Had you heard about Mr. Seselj yourself? Did you know who he was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I heard and saw on TV.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And who was it? You saw him on television, but what was the impression he gave you? Did he look like someone who could solve all problems? Did he look like an opponent to Milosevic? What impression did he convey?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, as far as I was concerned, he was just a politician like every other politician. I didn't have a bad opinion of anyone in the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't have a bad opinion that when I watched TV.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SESELJ
utterances.text: Okay. So who was this woman in Ruma who came to attend this meeting in Hrtkovci?

utterances.speaker: FRANJO BARICEVIC
